title: Still doing your bookkeeping once a year?
seo_title: Month-end close in 6 levels: a checklist for small businesses
description: A shoebox of receipts every April isn't bookkeeping. A real month-end close has six levels: bank feeds, categorizing, reconciliations, accruals, amortization and P&L analysis.
body: Plenty of business owners send their accountant a shoebox of receipts every April and call it bookkeeping. That isn't bookkeeping. It's a tax-season panic.
A real month-end close has six levels. If you only catch up once a year, you're skipping five of them, and you're making every decision in between on numbers that are months out of date.
## Level 1: Bank feeds

Every bank account and every card is connected to your accounting system, so not a single transaction goes missing. If an account isn't connected, its transactions only turn up when someone remembers to upload a statement.
## Level 2: Categorize

Every transaction is coded the same way, every month. Payroll is payroll. Software is software. When the same expense lands in a different account each month, your month-to-month comparisons stop meaning anything.
## Level 3: Reconciliations
This is how you know the books are actually right. Bank accounts, cards and loans have to match the books to the cent. If they don't, we find out why, before the month is closed, not a year later.
## Level 4: Accruals

Some bills haven't arrived yet when the month ends. Accruals record expenses and revenue in the month they actually happened, not when the invoice shows up. Without them, one month looks too good and the next looks too bad.
## Level 5: Amortization
Pay for a year of insurance or software upfront, and the cost is spread across all twelve months. Otherwise one month carries a huge expense and the other eleven look cheaper than they really are.
## Level 6: P&L analysis
This is what you actually get at the end: your reports by day 10 of the next month, compared with last month and with budget, with exactly what moved and why.
## Then it starts again
The point of all six levels is simple: you make decisions on this month's numbers, not last year's. And then the close starts again, every single month, in the same order.
Here's the quick checklist:
- **Bank feeds:** every account and card connected.
- **Categorize:** the same coding every month.
- **Reconciliations:** bank, cards and loans match to the cent.
- **Accruals:** costs and revenue in the month they happened.
- **Amortization:** big upfront payments spread over the months they cover.
- **P&L analysis:** reports by day 10, against last month and budget.

title: Do your Sage Intacct reports ever disagree?
seo_title: Sage Intacct dimension sprawl: why reports disagree and 5 steps to fix it
description: When Sage Intacct reports tell different stories, the cause is usually dimension sprawl: missing departments, duplicate locations and untagged lines. Five steps fix it for good.
body: Your P&L says one thing, the location report says another, and the board pack says something else again. In Sage Intacct, that's usually not a math problem. It's dimension sprawl.

Dimension sprawl looks like this: missing departments, duplicate locations and lines that were never tagged at all. Each report slices the same transactions a different way, so each one tells a slightly different story.
The good news: the numbers were never wrong. They just weren't tagged. Fix it in five levels, and every report tells the same story.
## Level 1: Map your dimensions
Agree what each dimension value means, and retire the duplicates nobody uses. If "NYC", "New York" and "NY Office" are all locations, pick one and merge the rest.
## Level 2: Make them required
Bills, invoices and journals can't post without a department and a location. Making dimensions required at entry is what stops new gaps from opening up.
## Level 3: Clean it up, once

Then deal with everything that's already untagged. Tag every line for the year, and reclass anything posted to the wrong place. It's a one-time job, and Level 2 makes sure you never have to do it again.
## Level 4: Report by dimension
Build the P&L, the location view and the board pack on the same tags. When every report reads from the same dimensions, they can't drift apart.
## Level 5: The close check
Add one rule to your month-end close: untagged lines have to hit zero before the month is closed. That's how you stop the sprawl coming back.
## The short version
Tag it once, check it every month, and every report agrees.

title: Why doesn't your Shopify payout match your sales?
seo_title: Why your Shopify payout doesn't match your sales (and how to reconcile it)
description: Shopify and Amazon payouts never match sales because fees, refunds and reserves come out first. Five steps, from a clearing account to A2X, make every dollar tie out.
body: Say your store sold $10,000 this week. The payout that lands in your bank is smaller, and it never seems to line up. That's one of the most common questions I get from eCommerce owners.
The answer: fees, refunds and reserves come out before the payout reaches your bank. The money's all there. It just arrives in pieces. Five levels, and every dollar ties out.
## Level 1: Split every payout
A payout isn't one number. Break each one into sales, discounts, refunds, fees and reserves, each on its own line. Once it's split, you can see exactly where the difference went.
## Level 2: Use a clearing account
Book sales to a clearing account, not straight to the bank. Each payout then clears that account. Anything left over is a real difference worth looking into, not noise.
## Level 3: Automate it with A2X
If you sell on Shopify and Amazon, you don't do this by hand. Connect A2X. It posts one summary per payout, per channel, already mapped to the right accounts.
## Level 4: Cost of goods
Book cost of goods in the same month as the sale, so your margin is real. Sales in one month with the product cost in another make both months wrong.
## Level 5: Reconcile
At month end, every payout matches a bank deposit, and the clearing account sits at zero. That's how you know it's right.
## The short version
The money was never missing. It just arrived in pieces. Split it, automate it, and every month ties out.
